lines.note: Fuxinauame names a manner of weaving or lacing armour. The scan reads tecedura, not tecedira; this meaning makes the rope-pattern compound plausible.
Armas completes the armour definition. This is a genuine short continuation row, with no Japanese headword omitted.
Fuxinqiû is a small bow; the final vowel is u with a circumflex, not ô. The enlarged-looking type and NINJAL agree on this uncommon printed long-u variant.
Fuxiqi, xirazu, is not knowing, with a Buddhist label. Xira is the regular dictionary shi-ra sequence, not a modern spelling imposed.

runs.text: Aruore caida com tormenta, ou de

lines.note: A different fuxiqi is a tree fallen in a storm. Its physical-tree sense is distinct from the preceding Buddhist ignorance.
The tree can also have fallen from rot and age. Cami introduces a regional usage; the name is wholly italic rather than only its first syllable.

runs.text: Aruore, ou pao de muitos noos.

lines.note: In Cami, fuxiqi is a tree or timber with many knots. This second sense fits fushi, knot, rather than the falling sense alone.
Fuxitauore is collapsing or falling to the ground. Cair is visible in the Portuguese, correcting the OCR's Cuir.
Fuxiuabi combines lying down and grieving or pleading. The historical uru/ita principal parts are preserved instead of replacing them with modern forms.
The gloss includes humbly begging and supplicating. The scan reads humildemente; the OCR's humeldemente is not retained.
Fuxiuogami is worshipping while prostrate. The entire Japanese headword is Roman; internal italic runs were spurious, and the printed ôda is retained.

runs.text: Quebradura polo nò como de aruo-

lines.note: Fuxiuore is breaking at a joint, such as in a tree. It is a nominal fracture definition, not the earlier verb of bowing down.
Tall plants are included in the joint-breaking gloss. Erua remains the historical form, not modern erva.
Fuxiutçubuqi is lying prone, with uita as the historical past abbreviation. Bruços confirms the posture; there is no reason to regularize the Japanese.
Fuxixizzumi is lying overwhelmed by sorrow. The worn principal part is ûda, supported by the remaining strokes and NINJAL; its u is not a Portuguese italic insertion.
The example begins qinu fiqicazzuite, covering oneself with silk. The ca is damaged; the enlarged remnants and covering gloss support it over fiqitazzuite. Joined grandetristeza is retained.
Namida no yuca ni is a floor or bed of tears; fuxixizzumarete is the respectful/passive-looking form. The worn c is retained as c, without inventing a different poetic noun.

runs.text: Estando cuberta com hum mãto de ſeda eſta-

lines.note: The Portuguese describes her covered with a silk mantle. The nasal contraction is mãto, not mẽto; the feminine cuberta is retained.

runs.text: ua com grande triſteza, & lagrimas deitada.

lines.note: She was lying in great grief and tears. This completes the silk-and-tears example, with the translation confirming the emotional rather than underwater sense.
The pilcrow begins another example, vomoi ni fuxi xizzumu, sinking under sorrow or longing. Its omission from OCR is repaired from the scan.

runs.text: ſo com tristeza, ou derrubado, & triſte de

lines.note: The Portuguese says submerged in sadness or cast down. Tristeza and derrubado restore the damaged but identifiable words; the u of derrubado is especially weak.
Amor completes the phrase: sadness caused by love. It qualifies the emotional example, not a separate headword.

runs.text: O meter no fundo a alguem com

lines.note: Fuxizzuqe is sinking someone with a weight. This dictionary definition records an action, without implying it is an instruction to perform it.
The stone is at the neck; fuxizzuqeni ſu- begins the corresponding verbal phrase. The Portuguese details confirm the immersion sense.
ru completes suru, then Item shifts to placing reeds or branches underwater. The common feature is submerging material, not necessarily the first sense's violence.

runs.text: ramos de aruore amarradas, & juntas dentro

lines.note: The branches or reeds are tied together. Amarradas and juntas are kept as printed despite the intervening masculine ramos.

runs.text: dagoa onde ſe recolhem os pexes com frio, &

lines.note: The submerged material shelters fish from cold. Pexes and dagoa retain historical spelling and joining.
Se tomão ends the fish-catching explanation. The very short row is part of that definition, not page furniture.
Fuxǒ is non-birth, paraphrased Vmarezu. The r is worn but recoverable in the enlargement; Vma ezu was an OCR omission and false space.
Fuxǒ fumet is neither arising nor perishing. Final t is retained as historical notation, not completed with an imagined vowel.
Another fuxǒ is an unsuccessful or unwanted result, paraphrased saiuaini arazu. The dictionary distinguishes this sense from non-birth.
The event does not go well or according to someone's will. Fuxǒ- begins an adjectival example on the next row.
Fuxǒna me ni vǒ is meeting misfortune. The contracted verb vǒ and the Portuguese encontrar agree; the accent is preserved.
The gloss includes trouble and displeasure, then begins a reluctant-action phrase. The two senses are explicitly related in the entry.
buxoni ſuru completes the reluctant phrase. The o in this occurrence lacks a clear mark, so no accent is supplied solely from the later fully accented headword.
Com repugnancia explains doing something unwillingly. The source's contracted algũa remains diplomatic rather than expanded.
Fuxô is not counting among capable people, paraphrased mono no cazu ni arazu. The circumflex distinguishes this printed form from the preceding caron forms.

runs.text: em numero. i, Não ter partes de letras ſa-

lines.note: The gloss concerns lacking literary and intellectual accomplishments. The explanatory i, is Portuguese metalanguage, not Japanese.
Fuxô no mi naredomo means although I am unworthy. Mi is self/body here; the quotation is a self-deprecating formula.

runs.text: Posto que eu não entre em numero de gente,

lines.note: Posto que introduces the concessive translation: although I do not count among people of worth. It should not be read as a physical location.
The speaker also disclaims accomplishments. This completes the modest formula and preserves partes in its older sense of abilities.
Fuxôbuxǒni is reluctantly, with two different visible long-o signs. The first circumflex was absent from OCR and is restored from the scan.
Acting contrary to desire and pleasure completes the reluctant-adverb gloss. No separate sense is inferred from the physical line break.
Fuxocu is lack of appetite, glossed Xocuxezu, not eating. The clear compound shoku-sezu corrects OCR's Xucinxezu; faſtio independently confirms it.
Fuxocu suru means having no appetite. The Japanese example and Portuguese ter faſtio agree directly.
Fuxôna and fuxǒna refer back to the two differently accented headwords. Both distinctions and the Japanese mata are retained.
The second cross-reference is Fuxǒ, with a weak but visible upper mark. It is not the short-vowel Fuxo produced by OCR.
Fuxubi, xubixezu, is inconsistency: beginning and end do not agree. The Portuguese discrepancia and the following promise example confirm the interpretation.
Fuxubina coto wo mǒsu is saying inconsistent things. Mǒsu's caron is visible and the verb remains respectful speech.

runs.text: que não concordão, como quando hum prome-

lines.note: The things said fail to agree; the example starts with someone promising. This is explanatory context, not a second Japanese quotation.

runs.text: teo algũa couſa, & de pois moſtra arrepen-

lines.note: After promising something, the person shows regret. De pois remains visibly separated; it is not modernized to depois.
derſe completes arrependerſe, to regret. The line break does not terminate the example prematurely.
Fuye, yaburazu, is not breaking or being destroyed. The printed des at the edge has no compulsory added hyphen.
Congǒ fuye is the unbreakable substance expression, glossed here as fine gold. This gloss is retained even though kongō has broader Buddhist associations.

runs.text: não ſe desfaz nem destrue por mais que o ba-

lines.note: The gold is not destroyed however much it is beaten. Destrue and desfaz are preserved as source forms.
tão completes batão. The nasal verb ending belongs to the beating example, not a new word.
Fuye is throat, a homophone of the flute sense below. Garganta is clear and does not warrant collapsing the entries.
Fuye is flute; Frauta, not Frauia, is the visible Portuguese word. Fuye wo fuqu means blowing/playing it.
The example combines sounding the tçuzzumi drum with the flute. Its second object continues fu-/ye across rows.
fuqitatetareba continues the sounding-up construction. The citation reads Tai. L. 28.; Tai. is Roman, L. 28. italic, and no absent f is added from the more usual Taif.
The drum-and-flute performance is translated directly. Tabaquinho is retained as the diminutive instrument term printed here.
Fuyeqi, cauarazu, is not changing. The ye represents the Japanese vowel sequence convention, not an extra modern syllable.
Fuyeqina coto is an immutable thing. The Portuguese immudauel spelling is historical and remains unchanged.
manente finishes permanente, reinforcing lasting immutability. This short continuation is not a separate Japanese form.
Fuyet is an axe, paraphrased Vono maſacari. Vono gives ono, and the scan's o corrects the OCR's Vuno.
Fuyô is the flower fuyō. The simple gloss does not justify adding a botanical species to the transcription.
Another Fuyô denotes laziness, with fuyô wo camayuru. The same long-o spelling need not imply the flower meaning.
Ter priguiça confirms laziness. The source's initial pri- is retained rather than changed to modern pre-.
Fuyo, with no long-o mark, is bestowing or distributing: cubari, atayuru. This is a meaning-bearing contrast with the previous long-vowel forms.
Fuyôna is the lazy adjective. The derivation and Portuguese priguiçoſo agree, and the circumflex is clearly printed.
Fuyù is a certain insect, distinct from short-vowel winter below. The grave-like u sign is retained and also occurs in the reference headword.
Fuyu is winter. Fuyu ni naru begins one of two expressions for its arrival.
fuyu qitaru supplies the alternative, winter comes. Qitaru corresponds to kitaru, and the seasonal meaning is explicit.
Fuyudachi is winter setting in. The Portuguese oinuerno is joined in the source, not automatically separated.
Fuyugomori means making winter preparations here. Its verbal paradigm is retained, rather than restricting the term to modern hibernation.
Apercebimento is preparing/provisioning for winter. The worn m is supported by the intact repetition below; the OCR's n and false internal space are corrected.
Fuyugomori is repeated as a noun with suru. The first u is clearly present, correcting Fayugomori.

runs.text: Fazer este aparelho, ou apercebimento como

lines.note: The preparations or supplies are explained further. The same apercebimento corroborates the damaged occurrence two rows above.

runs.text: de lenha, vestido, &c. pera o inuerno.

lines.note: Firewood and clothing are examples of winter supplies. Vestido is preserved rather than replaced with a modern plural.
Fuzacaxi means softening something by soaking, not the modern joking sense suggested by fuzakeru. The following water gloss governs the interpretation.
Nagoa demaſiadamente specifies excessive immersion. The joined preposition is retained as printed.
Fuzaqe is becoming damaged after too long in water. Its historical uru/eta paradigm is not modernized.

runs.text: & danarſe, ou apodrecer como bate, ma

lines.note: Bate and ma-/mes are food examples of rotting or spoiling. Bate is retained as visibly printed; this is not enough evidence to replace it with a more familiar word.

runs.text: mes, arroz cozido, &c. No Ximo ſe diz.

lines.note: Beans and cooked rice continue the food list. Ximo introduces the lower-region variant, with the visible capital X restored.
Fozaqe is the stated regional form. Its o is meaningful dialect evidence and is not normalized to Fuzaqe.
Fuyuzare is marked poetic and glossed fuyu no naca, midwinter. P. and explanatory i, are italic labels, while the Japanese remains Roman.
Inuerno completes midwinter. The preceding poetic label does not change this into another season.
Fuzô, maſazu, means not increasing. Vt, is italic as a whole; a stray Roman V had generated a false kana hint.
Fuzô fuguen is neither increasing nor diminishing, 不増不減. The final n of gen is present and belongs to the compound.
Fuzocu is handing over an inheritance or household. The first Portuguese fragment is he-, not be-, as confirmed by herança below.
The example begins voya no ixxeqi wo, the parent's hereditary place or estate. The inherited-property sense supports this Japanese expression.
coni fuzocuſuru transfers it to the child. The Portuguese reads pay, not poy, and states the father's bequest.

runs.text: ao filho. ¶ Item, O communicar ſaber, dou-

lines.note: Item extends the meaning to communicating knowledge. The faint c in communicar is recovered from the scan and the unmistakable syntax.
trina completes doutrina, followed by art conveyed to others. The first letter is t, not OCR's s; signature and catchword below are separate furniture.
